title: Guitar chords
subtitle: Strings, notes and the chords behind every song

cards.prompt: In standard tuning, what are the open strings from lowest (thickest) to highest (thinnest)?
cards.answer: E A D G B E
distractors: E A D G C E
D A D G B E
E A D F B E
cards.example: Before every practice session she tuned to E A D G B E and checked the high string last.
cards.note: A classic memory aid is 'Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie'. Both outer strings are E, two octaves apart.

cards.prompt: Which string do guitarists call the 6th string?
cards.example: Low E is the thickest string and sits closest to your chin when you hold the guitar.
cards.note: Strings are numbered from the thinnest (1st, high E) to the thickest (6th, low E). So the number counts up as the pitch goes down.

cards.prompt: Which note do you get at the 5th fret of the low E string?
cards.example: Press the low E string at the 5th fret and you hear an A, the same pitch as the open A string.
cards.note: This is the basis of the 5th fret tuning method: fret 5 on one string matches the next open string. The only exception is the G string, where you use fret 4 to match B.

cards.prompt: At which fret does a string sound exactly one octave higher than when played open?
cards.example: Most guitars mark the 12th fret with a double dot because the note names start over there.
cards.note: An octave has 12 semitones and each fret adds one, so fret 12 repeats the open note an octave up. That is why the fretboard pattern repeats after it.

cards.prompt: How far apart in pitch are two neighbouring frets?
cards.example: One semitone is what you gain each time your finger moves up a single fret.
cards.note: Twelve semitones make an octave. A whole tone is two frets, which is the distance from C to D.

cards.prompt: How many different notes make up a basic triad?
cards.example: Three different notes make a triad, even if you strum six strings and some of them repeat.
cards.note: A triad is a root, a third and a fifth stacked together. Open chords double some of these notes on several strings, which makes them sound fuller.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a C major chord?
cards.example: Every C major chord, open or barred, is built only from C E G.
cards.note: Root C, major third E (4 semitones up), fifth G (7 semitones up). C major uses only white piano keys, which makes it a handy reference chord.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a G major chord?
cards.example: The open G chord rings out with G B D spread across all six strings.
cards.note: Root G, major third B, fifth D. In the open shape the note G appears three times, which is why the chord sounds so big.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a D major chord?
cards.example: The small triangle shape of open D gives you D F# A on the top strings.
cards.note: The F# is the major third, 4 semitones above D. Lower it to F and the chord turns into D minor.

cards.prompt: Which notes form an A minor chord?
cards.example: A minor is spelled A C E, which even reads like the word ace.
cards.note: The C is a minor third, only 3 semitones above A. A minor has no sharps or flats, just like C major, because they share the same notes.

cards.prompt: Which notes form an E minor chord?
cards.example: With just two fingers down, open E minor already gives you E G B on all six strings.
cards.note: Three of the six open strings (E, G, B) are already chord tones. That is why E minor is often the very first chord beginners learn.

cards.prompt: Which notes form an E major chord?
cards.example: Add one finger to E minor on the G string and you get E G# B, the E major chord.
cards.note: Raising the third from G to G# turns minor into major. On the guitar that is a single finger on the 1st fret of the G string.

cards.prompt: Which notes form an A major chord?
cards.example: The three fingers lined up on the 2nd fret produce A C# E in the open A shape.
cards.note: Compare it with A minor (A C E): only the third moves up one semitone. That single note decides if a chord sounds bright or sad.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a D minor chord?
cards.example: Many sad ballads lean on D minor, whose notes are D F A.
cards.note: D minor is D major with the F# lowered to F. On the high E string that is one fret lower than in the D major shape.

cards.prompt: Which notes form an F major chord?
cards.example: Whether you play the full barre or the easy small version, F major is F A C.
cards.note: F major is often the first barre chord players meet. The notes F A C also spell FACE with the E in between, a common reading aid.

cards.prompt: Which chord tone is different between C major and C minor?
cards.example: The third is the only note that changes: E in C major, Eb in C minor.
cards.note: Root and fifth stay the same. The third alone gives a chord its major (bright) or minor (dark) character.

cards.prompt: How many semitones above the root is a minor third?
cards.example: From A up to C is 3 semitones, which is why A minor sounds minor.
cards.note: A major third is 4 semitones, a minor third is 3. On one string that is simply 3 frets versus 4 frets.

cards.prompt: Which two chord tones make up a power chord?
cards.example: Root and fifth are all a power chord needs, often with the root doubled an octave up.
cards.note: Without a third a power chord is neither major nor minor. That neutral sound stays clear under heavy distortion, which is why rock and metal love it.

cards.prompt: How is a power chord built on G usually written?
cards.example: The tab simply said G5, so he played the root on the low E string and the fifth two frets up on the A string.
cards.note: The 5 stands for the fifth, the only note added to the root. With no third, the chord is neither major nor minor, so the symbol leaves out m and maj.

cards.prompt: What is a chord called where one finger presses several strings flat across the same fret?
cards.example: Once you master one Barre chord shape, you can slide it up and down the neck to play any key.
cards.note: The index finger acts like a movable nut. An E-shape barre at fret 1 is F major, at fret 3 it is G major.

cards.prompt: With a capo on fret 2, an open G chord shape sounds like which chord?
cards.example: With the capo on fret 2 her G shape sounded as A major, matching the singer's key.
cards.note: A capo raises every string by one semitone per fret. G plus two semitones is A, so the shape stays the same while the key moves up.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a G7 chord?
cards.example: G7 adds an F to the triad, so its notes are G B D F.
cards.note: A plain 7 means a dominant seventh: the major triad plus a minor seventh (F, not F#). Its tension wants to resolve to C, which is why G7 so often leads home to C.

cards.prompt: Which notes form a Dsus4 chord?
cards.example: In Dsus4 the third is replaced, leaving D G A.
cards.note: Sus means suspended: the third is swapped for the fourth (G). Adding your pinky to the high E string at fret 3 turns D into Dsus4, a favourite folk flourish.

cards.prompt: In the key of G, which chords are I, IV and V?
cards.example: Countless campfire songs get by with nothing but G C D.
cards.note: Count up the G major scale: G is 1, C is 4, D is 5. The I IV V progression powers blues, folk and rock in every key.

cards.prompt: When you play an open D major chord, which strings do you strum?
cards.example: The four thinnest strings are all you strum for open D, starting from the open D string.
cards.note: The open D string is the root, so the chord starts there. Hitting the low E adds a note that is not in the chord and makes it sound muddy.
